As of 310 AM Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...  

1) A cold front will move across central NC today bringing showers 
and possible thunderstorms to the area. 

A cold front just east of the mountains attm will steadily move 
south and east today, reaching a position near the SC border and 
east toward the NC coast by this evening. Low- and mid-level 
moisture transport from the southwest ahead of the front will 
interact with this boundary resulting in one or more bands or rounds 
of showers and possible tstms which will develop invof the front, 
mainly along and south of the Hwy 64 corridor staring this afternoon 
and lasting off-and-on through this evening. Tstms chances will be 
highest south and east of RDU where fropa will occur later and the 
greatest prefrontal instability will be located. It's possible that 
some very localized minor poor drainage flooding could occur where 
cells train or brief heavy downpours occur, but that hazard risk 
looks fairly limited right now.  Otherwise, some light rain, more 
stratiform in nature on the cool stable side of the boundary, is 
also possible across our north and northwest zones later today and 
tonight, but given its light and patchy nature, will keep PoPs 
limited to chance through the daytime hours and slightly higher 
overnight as the cooler CAD regime continues to set up along with 
ongoing isentropic above the CAD. 

So in summary, highest tstm and localized flooding chances today and 
this evening across the southern half of central NC, with lighter 
amounts farther north and west in the cooler more stable airmass. 
It's worth noting that temps will be highly variable depending on 
where you are in relation to the front. High temps today will range 
from the lower 70s across the NW Piedmont to mid 80s across our far 
SE zones.


KEY MESSAGE 2... While periods of rain and cold air damming remain 
likely through the weekend, mesoscale influences from convection and 
related MCVs forecast to develop across the Carolinas through 
tonight may tend to suppress heavier, isentropically-driven rain on 
Sunday.

A positively-tilted trough and plume of deep moisture characterized 
by PWs 150-200% normal, evident in GOES-E water vapor satellite data 
from the Canadian Maritimes to Baja CA, will translate sewd and 
across the Southeast through early Mon. A series of convectively-
amplified mid-level disturbances from the Gulf to the Carolinas will 
track through the prevailing swly mid-level flow along and ahead of 
the trough. One such feature now over sern GA, and others that may 
develop in-situ within frontal convection forecast to develop across 
the Carolinas through tonight, will likely be in the process of 
exiting cntl NC by Sun morning, per an increasing signal of such in 
model guidance this morning. Following subsidence and veering of the 
flow to swly or even wly/nwly for a time, trailing the related 
low/mid-level vorticity maxima, will likely weaken what would 
otherwise be a favorable synoptic pattern of isentropic ascent over 
cntl NC on Sun. Another, probably larger disturbance originating 
from larger clusters of deep convection over the Gulf, will 
meanwhile track across the Gulf Coast and Southeast through Sun 
night. While this feature will likely enhance ascent and 
precipitation along its track, there are indications that a 
progressive nrn stream trough forecast to pivot across James Bay and 
surrounding ern Canada and Great Lakes will limit the nwwd extent of 
its related precipitation shield and possibly confine it to the srn 
and sern portions of NC later Sun through Sun night.  

At the surface, a wavy synoptic front and slightly preceding outflow 
boundary, now progressing swd across srn and cntl VA, will settle 
ssewd across cntl NC today, then become quasi-stationary across SC 
and southeastern NC later tonight and Sun. A following, ~1026-1028 
mb cP high now over the Great Lakes will progress across and 
offshore sern Canada through the weekend, while extending swd across 
the Middle Atlantic and Carolinas. Though progressive, the high will 
be favorably strong and located for cold air damming to develop over 
the srn Middle Atlantic and Carolinas. 

Given the mesoscale and subsequent nrn stream influences noted 
above, precipitation amounts have trended lower across model 
guidance in the past 24 hours for cntl NC, particularly over the 
Piedmont. While they may yet change further given remaining 
uncertainties on the mesoscale, there is greater confidence that 
precipitation amounts over the nw Piedmont, where the ongoing drought 
has become extreme to exceptional, may struggle to reach 0.50-0.75". 
Amounts in adjacent portions of the Piedmont may be similarly 
reduced if not impacted by convective, frontal precipitation prior 
to Sun. Meanwhile to the south and across the Sandhills and srn-cntl
